blocks.text: The very obscure passage on the ostrich, Iob. XXXIX, 16. var. 13., is explained

In Iobi XXXIX, 16. (var. 13.) the ostrich is described in six verses, of which the interpreters explain the last five after a fashion. But in the first they are so stuck that there is scarcely any passage of Scripture that is less understood. Nowhere is there greater disagreement among them, as will be clear from a comparison, which I am pleased to set out here so that the matter may be clearer to the reader. That verse, then, of which I speak, the Septuagint renders thus: Πτέρυξ τερπομένων νεέλασσα, ἐὰν συλλάβῃ ἀσίδα, καὶ νέσσα· [Pteryx terpomenōn neelassa, ean syllabē asida, kai nessa] The wing of those that rejoice is neelassa, if it has conceived asida and nessa. And Aquila: Πτερύγιον αἰνέντων συναναπλέκει . . . . ἐρώδιος, καὶ ἱέραξ· [Pterygion ainentōn synanaplekei . . . . erōdios, kai hierax] The heron and the hawk together entwine . . . . the wing of those that praise. And Symmachus: Πτερὸν ἀγλαισμοῦ περιφύεται, εἰ ἐναγκαλίσεται ὁ κύκνος πτίλους αὐτοῦ· [Pteron aglaismou periphyetai, ei enankalisetai ho kyknos ptilous autou] A wing of splendour grows round about, if the swan should clasp its feathers in its arms. And Jerome: The feather of the ostrich is like the feathers of the heron and the hawk. And the Syriac, which the Arabic mostly follows: ܒܓܦ ܡܫܒܚܢܐ ܡܬܪܘܡܐ ܘܦܪܚܐ ܘܐܬܝܐ ܘܡܩܢܢܐ, With wings of praises it is lifted up, and flies, and comes, and nests. And the Chaldee: גדפא דתרנגול דמשבחא ומקלסא ואין אברא דחוריתא ונוציציתא, The wing of the cock, which praises and celebrates: and is it the wing of the stork and the hawk? These versions of the ancients not only differ from one another δὶς διὰ πασῶν [dis dia pasōn], but most of them are also absurd and incongruous, and attribute to the sacred writer things that yield no suitable sense. Nor is there more agreement among some of the moderns. For Castalio has: Are the wings of the ostrich nobler, or the feathers and plumage of the stork? And Arias, quite differently and with no sense: The wing of those that exult is glad; or the feather of the stork, and plumage? And Junius, differently again: Would you give the wing to the peacocks to exult in, or the feather of the stork, or to the ostrich? Differently also the vernacular versions, I mean the French, English, Dutch and Italian: Have you given to the peacocks, or Do the peacocks have splendid wings through your work, or wings in which they exult? Have you given feathers and plumage to the ostrich? Since there is no leisure to examine each of these, it will suffice to deal with our vulgar version, which itself also does not seem accurate enough. For there are chiefly two things we find wanting in it. One, that it supplies too much that is not usually supplied, namely at the very beginning of the verse אם נתת, Have you given?, and the letter Lamed, the mark of the dative, before the words רננים and חסידה. The other, that it explains רננים renanim as peacocks, and חסידה chasida as ostrich; with neither of which can I agree. I shall therefore say what I think about the meaning of each word, so that the true meaning of the whole verse may emerge from it.
